Good, now I can actually see it. Verdict: **it holds up**, and better than I expected — but not because of the image alone.

**What's carrying it:**
- Every piece of live UI text sits on its own opaque surface — the search pill, the site/collection cards, the settings modal. None of it is rendered as bare text directly on the photo. That sidesteps the contrast problem I flagged earlier entirely; you don't need a scrim because nothing needs one.
- The section labels (`UNSORTED`, `EMBERSTONE`, `NEWS`) are the one exception — they *are* bare text over the image — and they happen to fall in the darker navy/tree/lake regions on the left, never crossing into the bright green band. That's either lucky layout or intentional, but it works.
- The `+` and gear circle buttons are semi-transparent dark discs, so they self-scrim wherever they land.

**One real risk, not hypothetical anymore:** those section labels are positioned by content, not by background luminance — if a user has more/fewer sections, or scrolls, a label could drift into the bright green swath (right where it peaks around x:400–900 in the upper half). Worth a quick check: do label rows have a `text-shadow` or backdrop under them, or are they relying purely on this one image's luck? If it's the latter, that's a latent bug waiting for a different background photo or a longer sidebar list — not urgent to fix now since you're locking this exact image in as default, but flag it for Coder as a "don't assume this everywhere" note if the theming logic gets reused.

Net: ship it, but add a one-line note to the task about the section-label contrast being position-dependent rather than guaranteed.

messages.content:
Directionally good — it's a natural extension of the appearance panel you already have (screen5), and blur-to-fade is the right mental model for "let the photo recede without losing it." A few things I'd think through before Coder builds it:

**Two sliders vs. one**
Transparency and blur are perceptually different controls (opacity/veil vs. focus), so keeping them separate is right — don't collapse into one "intensity" slider. But consider whether blur alone, cranked up, already gives you most of what a transparency slider gives you (softened, low-contrast background) — if so you may not need both to reach the useful range, and two redundant sliders is worse UX than one that does the job. Worth prototyping both extremes before committing to two controls.

**Fading to #fff/#000 — reconsider the endpoint**
A flat white/black overlay is the easy implementation, but it'll fight the image's own color temperature as it fades. The aurora is cool/blue-green; fading it to pure #fff in light mode will pass through a slightly muddy, color-shifted gray midpoint before going neutral. Two options:
- Fade to your theme's actual surface color (whatever `--bg-primary` resolves to) rather than literal #fff/#000 — keeps it consistent with the rest of the chrome instead of introducing a color that only exists in this one control.
- If you do want pure white/black, add a touch of blur *before* full opacity kicks in so the transition doesn't pass through a hard-edged, low-contrast smear at ~50%.

**Interaction with the sampled accent color**
Since accent color is canvas-sampled from the image (confirmed above), cranking transparency toward 100% will wash the image out — at some point there's nothing meaningful left to sample from, and the accent color should probably freeze at its last-sampled value rather than drift toward gray. Worth deciding that behavior explicitly rather than letting it happen by accident.

**Placement**
Put both sliders directly under the "Photos" background section in the existing modal (screen5), not as a separate section — they're modifiers of the current background choice, not a standalone feature, and should visually read as dependent/nested (e.g. indented or in a sub-panel) so it's clear they only apply when a photo background is active.

messages.content:
Makes sense — that's the cleaner conceptual boundary anyway. Colors/gradients are already flat, so a transparency slider fading toward another flat tone would be redundant with just picking a different swatch; blur wouldn't do anything to a flat color either (or if it's a gradient, blur would just soften the seam slightly, not worth the control). Restricting both sliders to photo backgrounds keeps the feature legible: "photos need taming, solids don't."

For the fade endpoint, since you're trying sampled-color first: fade to the sampled accent rather than a fixed neutral means the whole panel — background, accent color, and now the fade — all derive from one source. That's the more coherent system. If it looks muddy at high transparency (accent colors can get weird at low saturation/high blend ratios), black/white is a reasonable fallback exactly because it's predictable and neutral, just less "of the image." Good to hold both as options and eyeball it rather than deciding blind.

One implementation note worth flagging to Coder either way: the fade target should probably be computed once when the photo/accent is set, not re-sampled live as the slider moves — re-sampling per-frame while dragging could be janky or expensive depending on how the canvas sampling is implemented.

Sounds like this is ready to hand off — want me to add these details (sliders scoped to Photos section only, fade-to-sampled-accent with black/white fallback, sample-once-not-live) as a comment on the in-review task, or should this be a new task since it's a different feature from the aurora swap?
I would push back on that last point and say that it SHOULD be sampled live. Otherwise the user would just have to guess and keep opening/closing settings to get it right.

messages.content:
Fair pushback — I stated that badly. I didn't mean the slider shouldn't preview live; a transparency/blur control with no live feedback would be useless, agreed. What I meant is narrower: the canvas pixel-sampling operation that *extracts* the accent color from the image is the potentially expensive part, and that only needs to run once when the photo is selected — not re-run on every slider tick.

Once that color is sampled and cached, dragging the slider is just interpolating CSS `opacity`/`filter: blur()` toward that already-known value — which is cheap and should absolutely update live, no guessing, no reopening settings. So: live slider feedback, yes; live re-sampling of the source image on every pixel of drag, no — those are two different operations and only the second one needs throttling.
Oh, yes. There's no reason to be constantly resampling the accent color because that's not changing with the sliders.

messages.content: What do you think about making the bookmarks bar a grid? Useful or no?
messages.editable_content: What do you think about making the bookmarks bar a grid? Useful or no?

messages.content:
Depends on what problem you're solving — worth separating two different use cases before deciding:

**If it's still living inside that same dropdown panel** (the one from screen3, alongside Open Tabs and History, all triggered from the same search bar): I'd lean **no**. That panel's whole interaction model is a scannable, keyboard-navigable list — arrow down, hit enter, or type to filter. Rows there show favicon + full title, which matters for bookmarks especially since names vary a lot in length and aren't always recognizable by icon alone (a lot of favicons are near-identical colored squares/letters). Switching just the Bookmarks Bar section to a grid while Open Tabs/History stay lists means the user learns two different navigation patterns in one control, and you'd have to either truncate titles hard or drop them to icon-only — losing exactly the "read the name to disambiguate" advantage a list gives you.

**If you're thinking of a separate favorites/speed-dial surface** (e.g., its own view, more visual, closer to a new-tab speed-dial grid): then yes, a grid is the right call — that's a fundamentally different task (glance-and-click on a small, memorized set) rather than search-and-select from a longer list, and icon-forward grids are proven for that (every browser's own speed dial works this way).

So: same panel, keep it a list for consistency and text-scanability. Separate feature, grid makes sense. Which one did you have in mind?
Eh, it's not necessary. Commit and push.
